claim: A low number of individuals show an atypical brain control of language functions that differs from the typical lateralization in the left cerebral hemisphere.
source: A low number of individuals show an atypical brain control of language functions that differs from the typical lateralization in the left cerebral hemisphere.
evidence: This is a general statement about atypical language lateralization, supported by established scientific knowledge and citations provided later in the manuscript.

claim: Using an fMRI-adapted stop-signal task in a healthy non right-handed sample (50 typically lateralized and 36 atypically lateralized for language production), atypical lateralization is associated with a mirrored brain organization of the inhibitory control network in the left hemisphere: inferior frontal cortex, presupplementary motor area, and subthalamic nucleus.
source: Using an fMRI-adapted stop-signal task in a healthy non right-handed sample (50 typically lateralized and 36 atypically lateralized for language production), our results show that atypical lateralization is associated with a mirrored brain organization of the inhibitory control network in the left hemisphere: inferior frontal cortex, presupplementary motor area, and subthalamic nucleus.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from the fMRI study described in the manuscript.

claim: Individual analyses revealed a large number of cases with a noteworthy overlap in the inferior frontal gyrus, which shared both inhibitory and language functions.
source: However, the individual analyses revealed a large number of cases with a noteworthy overlap in the inferior frontal gyrus, which shared both inhibitory and language functions.
evidence: This is supported by individual-level data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Atypical lateralization was associated with stronger functional interhemispheric connectivity.
source: Further analyses showed that atypical lateralization was associated with stronger functional interhemispheric connectivity and larger corpus callosum.
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Atypical lateralization was associated with larger corpus callosum.
source: Further analyses showed that atypical lateralization was associated with stronger functional interhemispheric connectivity and larger corpus callosum.
evidence: This is supported by structural MRI data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There were no task performance differences as a function of lateralization.
source: Importantly, we did not find task performance differences as a function of lateralization, but there was an association between atypical dominance in the inferior frontal cortex and higher scores on schizotypy and autistic spectrum traits, as well as worse performance on a reading accuracy test.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis showing no significant differences in task performance between groups.

claim: There was an association between atypical dominance in the inferior frontal cortex and higher scores on schizotypy traits.
source: Importantly, we did not find task performance differences as a function of lateralization, but there was an association between atypical dominance in the inferior frontal cortex and higher scores on schizotypy and autistic spectrum traits, as well as worse performance on a reading accuracy test.
evidence: This is supported by correlational analyses between lateralization indices and SPQ scores.

claim: There was an association between atypical dominance in the inferior frontal cortex and higher scores on autistic spectrum traits.
source: Importantly, we did not find task performance differences as a function of lateralization, but there was an association between atypical dominance in the inferior frontal cortex and higher scores on schizotypy and autistic spectrum traits, as well as worse performance on a reading accuracy test.
evidence: This is supported by correlational analyses between lateralization indices and AQ scores.

claim: There was an association between atypical dominance in the inferior frontal cortex and worse performance on a reading accuracy test.
source: Importantly, we did not find task performance differences as a function of lateralization, but there was an association between atypical dominance in the inferior frontal cortex and higher scores on schizotypy and autistic spectrum traits, as well as worse performance on a reading accuracy test.
evidence: This is supported by correlational analyses between lateralization indices and reading test performance.

claim: The brain control of language is lateralized to the left hemisphere.
source: One of the oldest findings in human neuroscience is that the brain control of language is lateralized to the left hemisphere (Broca, 1861; Wernicke, 1874; Price, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by historical citations and established scientific knowledge.

claim: 22–24% of left-handers show an atypical lateralization of language – right or ambilateral.
source: Some left-handers (22–24%) show an atypical lateralization of language – right or ambilateral (Pujol et al., 1999; Szaflarski et al., 2002; Mazoyer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Atypical language organization is observed in some neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia, dyslexia, or autistic spectrum.
source: Also, this atypical organization is observed in some neurodevelopmental disorders such as schizophrenia, dyslexia, or autistic spectrum (Bishop, 2013; Sommer et al., 2001; Eyler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: The Causal hypothesis argues that rapid activities requiring the implementation of sequences of cognitive processes are better performed from a single, unilateral control.
source: The Causal hypothesis (Kosslyn, 1987; Hellige, 1990) argues that rapid activities requiring the implementation of sequences of cognitive processes are better performed from a single, unilateral control.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: According to the Causal hypothesis, some functions will be performed better if they are controlled by different hemispheres.
source: As a result, these activities are innately programmed to be lateralized, and, according to this model, some functions will be performed better if they are controlled by different hemispheres.
evidence: This is an inference from the Causal hypothesis described in the manuscript.

claim: Language production predominantly lateralizes to the left hemisphere, while visuospatial attention typically favors the right hemisphere.
source: For example, language production predominantly lateralizes to the left hemisphere, while visuospatial attention typically favors the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about hemispheric specialization.

claim: According to the Causal hypothesis, if language were to atypically lateralize to the right hemisphere, visuospatial attention would, in turn, shift to the left hemisphere.
source: As per the Causal hypothesis, if language were to atypically lateralize to the right hemisphere, visuospatial attention would, in turn, shift to the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the Causal hypothesis.

claim: The Statistical hypothesis postulates that each cognitive function lateralizes independently from the others.
source: The Statistical hypothesis (Bryden et al., 1983), on the other hand, postulates that each cognitive function lateralizes independently from the others.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Some studies have obtained data favoring the Statistical hypothesis when analyzing language, visuospatial attention, and face processing.
source: Some studies have obtained data favoring the Statistical hypothesis when analyzing language, visuospatial attention, and face processing (Whitehouse and Bishop, 2009; Badzakova-Trajkov et al., 2010; Rosch et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Most investigations have demonstrated a mirrored organization of praxis in most individuals with atypical lateralization of language.
source: Most investigations, however, have demonstrated a mirrored organization of praxis (Vingerhoets et al., 2013; Gerrits et al., 2020), visuospatial attention (Badzakova-Trajkov et al., 2010; Gerrits et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2013), face recognition (Badzakova-Trajkov et al., 2010; Gerrits et al., 2020; Gerrits et al., 2019), and emotional prosody (Gerrits et al., 2020) in most individuals with atypical lateralization of language.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies.

claim: Most investigations have demonstrated a mirrored organization of visuospatial attention in most individuals with atypical lateralization of language.
source: Most investigations, however, have demonstrated a mirrored organization of praxis (Vingerhoets et al., 2013; Gerrits et al., 2020), visuospatial attention (Badzakova-Trajkov et al., 2010; Gerrits et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2013), face recognition (Badzakova-Trajkov et al., 2010; Gerrits et al., 2020; Gerrits et al., 2019), and emotional prosody (Gerrits et al., 2020) in most individuals with atypical lateralization of language.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies.

claim: Most investigations have demonstrated a mirrored organization of face recognition in most individuals with atypical lateralization of language.

evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies.

claim: Most investigations have demonstrated a mirrored organization of emotional prosody in most individuals with atypical lateralization of language.
source: Most investigations, however, have demonstrated a mirrored organization of praxis (Vingerhoets et al., 2013; Gerrits et al., 2020), visuospatial attention (Badzakova-Trajkov et al., 2010; Gerrits et al., 2020; Cai et al., 2013), face recognition (Badzakova-Trajkov et al., 2010; Gerrits et al., 2020; Gerrits et al., 2019), and emotional prosody (Gerrits et al., 2020) in most individuals with atypical lateralization of language.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies.

claim: The reversed pattern of mirrored organization is not observed in all atypical participants.
source: Nonetheless, it should be noted that this reversed pattern is not observed in all atypical participants, and all the studies found specific cases in favor of both theories (Gerrits et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Stopping an ongoing response involves a rightward network that includes the IFC, presupplementary motor area (preSMA), and subthalamic nucleus (STN).
source: According to previous literature, this function would be inhibitory control. Extensive results support the notion that stopping an ongoing response involves a rightward network that includes the IFC, presupplementary motor area (preSMA), and subthalamic nucleus (STN) (Aron and Poldrack, 2006; Xue et al., 2008; Aron et al., 2014; Hannah and Aron, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple research studies on inhibitory control.

claim: No investigation to date has analyzed the relationship between inhibitory control and language production lateralization.
source: Thus, inhibitory control and language production together are the ideal candidates to investigate the Causal vs. Statistical disjunctive. But surprisingly, no investigation to date has analyzed this.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research, which can be inferred from the literature review.

claim: Atypical lateralization of language has been found to be a defining characteristic among patients of dyslexia.
source: In clinical populations, atypical lateralization of language has been found to be a defining characteristic among patients of dyslexia (Bishop, 2013), schizophrenia (Sommer et al., 2001), and autism spectrum disorders (Eyler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Atypical lateralization of language has been found to be a defining characteristic among patients of schizophrenia.
source: In clinical populations, atypical lateralization of language has been found to be a defining characteristic among patients of dyslexia (Bishop, 2013), schizophrenia (Sommer et al., 2001), and autism spectrum disorders (Eyler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Atypical lateralization of language has been found to be a defining characteristic among patients of autism spectrum disorders.
source: In clinical populations, atypical lateralization of language has been found to be a defining characteristic among patients of dyslexia (Bishop, 2013), schizophrenia (Sommer et al., 2001), and autism spectrum disorders (Eyler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Individuals with atypical language lateralization exhibit poorer language performance.
source: However, aside from exhibiting poorer language performance (Mellet et al., 2014; Powell et al., 2012), no study to date has identified subclinical markers of these neurodevelopmental conditions among healthy individuals with atypical lateralization.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: No study to date has identified subclinical markers of neurodevelopmental conditions among healthy individuals with atypical lateralization.
source: However, aside from exhibiting poorer language performance (Mellet et al., 2014; Powell et al., 2012), no study to date has identified subclinical markers of these neurodevelopmental conditions among healthy individuals with atypical lateralization.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research findings.

claim: Regional functional lateralization is directly linked to the size reduction of its interconnecting corpus callosum segments.
source: Regarding the neural basis of language lateralization, the corpus callosum hypothesis (Gazzaniga, 2000)— which suggests that typical hemispheric specialization relies on the proper development of this structure — has garnered attention in recent years due to several noteworthy findings: (1) regional functional lateralization is directly linked to the size reduction of its interconnecting corpus callosum segments (Karolis et al., 2019); and (2) atypical lateralization of language has been associated with a larger corpus callosum and increased interhemispheric transfer at rest in language-relevant regions (Labache et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Atypical lateralization of language has been associated with a larger corpus callosum and increased interhemispheric transfer at rest in language-relevant regions.
source: Regarding the neural basis of language lateralization, the corpus callosum hypothesis (Gazzaniga, 2000)— which suggests that typical hemispheric specialization relies on the proper development of this structure — has garnered attention in recent years due to several noteworthy findings: (1) regional functional lateralization is directly linked to the size reduction of its interconnecting corpus callosum segments (Karolis et al., 2019); and (2) atypical lateralization of language has been associated with a larger corpus callosum and increased interhemispheric transfer at rest in language-relevant regions (Labache et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All four structures (pars opercularis, pars triangularis, preSMA, STN) displayed a statistically significant Hemisphere × Group interaction.
source: Examination of the simple effects across each level of Region revealed that all the tested structures displayed a statistically significant Hemisphere × Group interaction (pars opercularis F1,84=25.59, p<0.001; pars triangularis F1,84=19.95, p<0.001; preSMA F1,84=7.63, p=0.028; STN F1,84=14.24, p<0.001; p values Bonferroni-adjusted; see Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Depending on the lateralization group, all four regions appeared to exhibit a leftward (atypical group) or rightward (typical group) lateralization of their BOLD signal during the 'correct stop >correct go' condition of the stop-signal task.
source: In other words, depending on the lateralization group, all four regions appeared to exhibit a leftward (atypical group) or rightward (typical group) lateralization of their BOLD signal during the 'correct stop >correct go' condition of the stop-signal task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results from the fMRI data.

claim: Two-sample t-test comparisons of the typical and atypical groups during the 'correct stop >correct go' condition showed a differential asymmetry pattern in all the ROI-corresponding areas.
source: Two-sample t-test comparisons of the typical and atypical groups during the 'correct stop >correct go' condition showed a differential asymmetry pattern in all the ROI-corresponding areas, while also revealing differences in other cortical and subcortical regions, including the angular gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and caudate (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by voxel-wise whole-brain analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The typical group presented a rightward activity in the angular gyrus, middle temporal gyrus, and caudate, whereas the atypical group exhibited a leftward shift.
source: Specifically, the typical group presented a rightward activity in these regions, whereas the atypical group exhibited a leftward shift (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The Pearson's correlation between the frontal LIs (pars opercularis + pars triangularis) from the verb generation task and the stop-signal task revealed a strong inverse correlation (r84 = −0.58; two-tailed p<0.001; R2=0.34).
source: Finally, the Pearson's correlation between the frontal LIs (pars opercularis + pars triangularis) from the verb generation task and the stop-signal task revealed a strong inverse correlation (r84 = −0.58; two-tailed p<0.001; R2=0.34) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlational analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Out of 50 typically lateralized for language, 33 (66%) presented a typical right lateralization for inhibitory control, and 17 (34%) showed an atypical (left – ambilateral) lateralization.
source: Out of 50 typically lateralized for language, 33 (66%) presented a typical right lateralization for inhibitory control, and 17 (34%) showed an atypical (left – ambilateral) lateralization.
evidence: This is supported by individual-level data analysis.

claim: Among the 36 individuals from the atypical group, only 8 (22.2%) presented a typical lateralization during the stop-signal task, whereas 28 (77.8%) showed an atypical lateralization.
source: Among the 36 individuals from the atypical group, only 8 (22.2%) presented a typical lateralization during the stop-signal task, whereas 28 (77.8%) showed an atypical lateralization.

claim: No participant presented a leftward + leftward or rightward + rightward segregation pattern for language production and response inhibition.
source: Importantly, no participant presented a leftward + leftward or rightward + rightward segregation pattern for language production and response inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by individual-level data analysis.

claim: Strong segregation of both functions into different hemispheres was observed in 38 participants (44.2%).
source: Strong segregation of both functions into different hemispheres was observed in 38 participants (44.2%).
evidence: This is supported by individual-level data analysis.

source: The remaining 48 individuals (55.8%) presented an ambilateral representation of one or both functions, with an important level of spatial overlap in their activations (see Figure 1d).

claim: In the ambilateral group, language production presented an overlap in 32.3% of its voxels in the left hemisphere, and in 58.6% of its voxels in the right hemisphere.
source: In this ambilateral group, language production presented an overlap in 32.3% of its voxels in the left hemisphere, and in 58.6% of its voxels in the right hemisphere.

source: Inhibitory control showed an overlap in 57.2% of its voxels in the left hemisphere, and in 22.8% of its voxels of the right hemisphere.

claim: Volume in the genu, body and splenium of the corpus callosum was inversely related with language LI (respectively: ρ83 = −0.25, p=0.02; ρ83 = −0.26, p=0.02; and ρ83 = −0.25, p=0.02).
source: Volume in the genu, body and splenium of the corpus callosum was inversely related with language LI (respectively: ρ83 = −0.25, p=0.02; ρ83 = −0.26, p=0.02; and ρ83 = −0.25, p=0.02).

claim: Only the callosal genu was found related with inhibition LI (ρ83=0.25, p=0.02).
source: However, only the callosal genu was found related with inhibition LI (ρ83=0.25, p=0.02).

claim: The volume of the callosal genu increased as functional organization of the IFC became more atypical.
source: That is, the volume of the callosal genu increased as functional organization of the IFC became more atypical, extending this effect to the whole corpus callosum when considering exclusively language lateralization.

claim: VMHC of the pars triangularis increased as a function of inhibition LI (ρ77=0.26, p=0.02).
source: On the same line, ROI interhemispheric functional connectivity analyses at rest revealed that VMHC of the pars triangularis also increased as a function of inhibition LI (ρ77=0.26, p=0.02), but a similar relation failed to be found for language LI (ρ77 = −0.12, p=0.3).
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis of resting-state fMRI data.

claim: A similar relation between VMHC of the pars triangularis and language LI failed to be found (ρ77 = −0.12, p=0.3).
source: On the same line, ROI interhemispheric functional connectivity analyses at rest revealed that VMHC of the pars triangularis also increased as a function of inhibition LI (ρ77=0.26, p=0.02), but a similar relation failed to be found for language LI (ρ77 = −0.12, p=0.3).
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis showing no significant correlation.

claim: No statistically significant linear relationships were found when exploring the VMHC of the pars opercularis, the preSMA, or the STN.
source: No statistically significant linear relationships were found when exploring the VMHC of the pars opercularis, the preSMA, or the STN.

source: It should be mentioned, however, that the association between VMHC of the STN and inhibition LI was close to significance (ρ77=0.22, p=0.054).
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analysis showing a trend toward significance.

source: Behaviorally, performance (RT, SSRT, and accuracy) during the scanner stop-signal task did not correlate with language and inhibition LIs.

source: Regarding the reading test, accuracy for word length and word familiarity were found correlated with both LIs (length and language: ρ84 = −0.24, p=0.03; length and inhibition: ρ84=0.21, p=0.04; familiarity and language: ρ84 = −0.23, p=0.03; familiarity and inhibition: ρ84=0.3, p=0.01).

evidence: This is supported by correlational analysis of behavioral data.

source: Regarding the reading test, accuracy for word length and word familiarity were found correlated with both LIs (length and language: ρ84 = −0.24, p=0.03; length and inhibition: ρ84=0.21, p=0.04; familiarity and language: ρ84 = −0.23, p=0.03; familiarity and inhibition: ρ84=0.3, p=0.01).

source: AQ, on the other hand, presented an association with language LI (ρ84 = −0.25, p=0.02) but not with inhibition LI (ρ84=0.0.8, p=0.5).

claim: AQ did not present an association with inhibition LI (ρ84=0.0.8, p=0.5).
source: AQ, on the other hand, presented an association with language LI (ρ84 = −0.25, p=0.02) but not with inhibition LI (ρ84=0.0.8, p=0.5).
evidence: This is supported by correlational analysis showing no significant relationship.

claim: This is the first demonstration that an entire cerebral network controlling a cognitive function shows a completely flipped organization in an atypical population for language.
source: Thus, this is the first demonstration that an entire cerebral network controlling a cognitive function shows a completely flipped organization in an atypical population for language, which supports the Causal hypothesis of lateralization (Kosslyn, 1987; Hellige, 1990).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, inferred from the literature review and current results.

claim: The results support the Causal hypothesis of lateralization.
source: Thus, this is the first demonstration that an entire cerebral network controlling a cognitive function shows a completely flipped organization in an atypical population for language, which supports the Causal hypothesis of lateralization (Kosslyn, 1987; Hellige, 1990).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of theoretical frameworks.

claim: Hemispheric lateralization goes beyond cerebral cortices and interhemispheric connectivity through the corpus callosum, as it also involves frontal-subcortical circuits.
source: Moreover, this result reveals that hemispheric lateralization goes beyond cerebral cortices, and even interhemispheric connectivity, through the corpus callosum, given that it also involves frontal-subcortical circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that subcortical structures also show lateralization patterns.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated a significantly higher involvement of the left IFC during cognitive control tasks in bilingual individuals when compared to monolinguals.
source: It should be noted that previous studies have demonstrated a significantly higher involvement of the left IFC during cognitive control tasks in bilingual individuals when compared to monolinguals (Garbin et al., 2010; Rodríguez-Pujadas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Bilingualism could be acting as an enabling mechanism among atypically lateralized participants for the shift of the inhibitory control network to the left hemisphere.
source: So, we cannot rule out the possibility that bilingualism could be acting as an enabling mechanism among atypically lateralized participants for the shift of the inhibitory control network to the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential confounding factor.

claim: Brain organization for language and inhibition, as initially defined in the study, and cognitive efficiency are not directly related.
source: Thus, brain organization for language and inhibition, as initially defined in our study, and cognitive efficiency are not directly related, based on our data.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that performance did not differ between groups.

claim: A densely segregated functional organization, rather than a reversed organization, is linked to general cognitive deficits.
source: This finding is consistent with prior studies highlighting that: (1) a densely segregated functional organization, rather than a reversed organization, is linked to general (Gerrits et al., 2020) and specific (Mellet et al., 2014) cognitive deficits; and (2) specific cognitive deficits appear to be confined to the domains of verbal and spatial skills (Mellet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Specific cognitive deficits appear to be confined to the domains of verbal and spatial skills.
source: This finding is consistent with prior studies highlighting that: (1) a densely segregated functional organization, rather than a reversed organization, is linked to general (Gerrits et al., 2020) and specific (Mellet et al., 2014) cognitive deficits; and (2) specific cognitive deficits appear to be confined to the domains of verbal and spatial skills (Mellet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The vast majority of hemispherically segregated individuals showed the typical segregation of language in the left hemisphere and inhibitory control in the right hemisphere.
source: The vast majority of hemispherically segregated individuals showed the typical segregation of language in the left hemisphere and inhibitory control in the right hemisphere, whereas only a low percentage displayed the opposite segregated organization.
evidence: This is supported by individual-level data analysis.

claim: Only a low percentage of hemispherically segregated individuals displayed the opposite segregated organization (language in right, inhibition in left).
source: The vast majority of hemispherically segregated individuals showed the typical segregation of language in the left hemisphere and inhibitory control in the right hemisphere, whereas only a low percentage displayed the opposite segregated organization.
evidence: This is supported by individual-level data analysis.

claim: Typical right hemispheric functions (such as inhibition) seem to be more bilaterally represented than typical left functions (such as language).
source: Both the low ratio of atypical segregation and the high ratio of bilateral inhibitory control could be explained by the fact that typical right hemispheric functions (such as inhibition) seem to be more bilaterally represented than typical left functions (such as language; Gotts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and used to explain the current findings.

claim: A strong atypical segregation of the two functions is possible, although infrequent.
source: Some conclusions can be extracted from this: (1) Although infrequent, a strong atypical segregation of the two functions is possible;
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the individual-level data analysis.

claim: The data have not revealed any case with a segregation of both frontal cognitive functions in the same hemisphere.
source: (2) Our data have not revealed any case with a segregation of both frontal cognitive functions in the same hemisphere;
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the individual-level data analysis.

claim: A large percentage of participants with a strong left lateralization of language presented a bilateral control of inhibition.
source: and (3) A large percentage of participants with a strong left lateralization of language presented a bilateral control of inhibition, showing that a typical dominance for language does not imply a strongly lateralized organization of other cognitive functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the individual-level data analysis.

claim: A typical dominance for language does not imply a strongly lateralized organization of other cognitive functions.
source: and (3) A large percentage of participants with a strong left lateralization of language presented a bilateral control of inhibition, showing that a typical dominance for language does not imply a strongly lateralized organization of other cognitive functions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that many typical language participants had bilateral inhibition.

claim: The existence of exceptions to the group pattern of mirrored brain organization requires caution when interpreting these data as supporting the causal hypothesis.
source: The existence of exceptions to the group pattern of mirrored brain organization requires us to use caution when interpreting these data as supporting the causal hypothesis.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement based on the variability in individual data.

claim: Some individual data support the statistical hypothesis instead of the causal hypothesis.
source: Although the negative correlation between the lateralization indexes during the verb generation task and the stop-signal task is strong at the group level, some individual data support the statistical hypothesis (Bryden et al., 1983) instead.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the individual variability in the data.

claim: Causal-supporting vs. statistical-supporting results reflect two different pathways to cognitive control: the segregated pathway and the integrated pathway.
source: Given that we found no cases of both cognitive functions completely sharing a hemisphere (see Figure 2), we propose that causal-supporting vs. statistical-supporting results reflects two different pathways to cognitive control. On the one hand, the segregated pathway (in line with the Causal hypothesis) develops due to the cerebral bias towards lateralizing certain cognitive functions in a single hemisphere. On the other hand, the integrated pathway (in line with the Statistical hypothesis), appears when ontogenetic development towards strong lateralized control fails in some way.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal based on the pattern of results observed.

claim: The segregated pathway develops due to the cerebral bias towards lateralizing certain cognitive functions in a single hemisphere.
source: On the one hand, the segregated pathway (in line with the Causal hypothesis) develops due to the cerebral bias towards lateralizing certain cognitive functions in a single hemisphere.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the segregated pattern observed.

claim: The integrated pathway appears when ontogenetic development towards strong lateralized control fails in some way.
source: On the other hand, the integrated pathway (in line with the Statistical hypothesis), appears when ontogenetic development towards strong lateralized control fails in some way.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the integrated pattern observed.

claim: A left-sided lesion in an individual with rightward language lateralization may result in inhibitory control and social deficits.
source: For example, a left-sided lesion in an individual with rightward language lateralization may result in inhibitory control and social deficits (Mosch et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The genu area of the corpus callosum is responsible for the connectivity between the two inferior frontal gyri.
source: The corpus callosum is the main cerebral structure in interhemispheric connectivity, with the genu area being responsible for the connectivity between the two inferior frontal gyri (Hofer and Frahm, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research on neuroanatomy.

claim: Phylogenetic data have demonstrated a negative association between the corpus callosum volume and hemispheric specialization.
source: Phylogenetic data have demonstrated a negative association between the corpus callosum volume and hemispheric specialization, suggesting that the ontogenetic development of the brain is supported by a decrease in interhemispheric connectivity to potentiate and establish intrahemispheric connectivity and hemispheric specialization (Tzourio-Mazoyer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The ontogenetic development of the brain is supported by a decrease in interhemispheric connectivity to potentiate and establish intrahemispheric connectivity and hemispheric specialization.
source: Phylogenetic data have demonstrated a negative association between the corpus callosum volume and hemispheric specialization, suggesting that the ontogenetic development of the brain is supported by a decrease in interhemispheric connectivity to potentiate and establish intrahemispheric connectivity and hemispheric specialization (Tzourio-Mazoyer, 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by a citation.

claim: There is evidence of the mechanism of decreased interhemispheric connectivity in language development.
source: There is evidence of this mechanism in language development (Tzourio-Mazoyer and Seghier, 2016) and in agenesis of the corpus callosum, which has been associated with lower lateralization of language and worse language performance (Hinkley et al., 2016; Bartha-Doering et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Agenesis of the corpus callosum has been associated with lower lateralization of language and worse language performance.
source: There is evidence of this mechanism in language development (Tzourio-Mazoyer and Seghier, 2016) and in agenesis of the corpus callosum, which has been associated with lower lateralization of language and worse language performance (Hinkley et al., 2016; Bartha-Doering et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The study replicated the relation between callosal enlargement and atypical functional organization found in a previous study.
source: In line with this proposal, we have replicated the relation between callosal enlargement and atypical functional organization found in a previous study (Labache et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim about replication of previous findings, supported by the current data and a citation.

claim: The structural correlation between callosal enlargement and atypical organization was accompanied by an association between atypical lateralization of inhibitory control and strength of interhemispheric functional connectivity in the pars triangularis of the IFC.
source: Moreover, in our data, this structural correlation was accompanied by an association between atypical lateralization of inhibitory control and strength of interhemispheric functional connectivity in the pars triangularis of the IFC.
evidence: This is supported by the functional connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Atypical organizations were found linearly related with higher scores on a schizotypy test (only for inhibitory control).
source: As hypothesized, when considering the functional lateralization during both tasks, atypical organizations were found linearly related with higher scores on a schizotypy test (only for inhibitory control), higher scores on an autistic spectrum test (only for language production), and a higher rate of reading errors (both language production and inhibitory control).
evidence: This is supported by correlational analysis of questionnaire data.

source: The first result is consistent with previous structural, functional, and behavioral data that have shown reduced language lateralization in schizophrenia patients (Sommer et al., 2001; Li et al., 2007).
